newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge formally endorses Valdez verdict.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge formally endorses Valdez verdict.

text.p: A federal judge on Tuesday entered formal judgment on the $5 billion fine slapped on Exxon Corp by a jury two years ago as punishment for the disastrous 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill.

U.S. District Court Judge H. Russel Holland approved the punitive fine -- the largest assessed by a jury against a corporation -- along with compensation to commercial fishermen, accrued interest and a $5,000 punitive fine against former Exxon supertanker captain Joseph Hazelwood.
The entry of judgment ended years of litigation at the District Court level, one plaintiff attorney said.

"This is the principle goal to which we have been striving for the last 7 1/2 years," said Dave Oesting, a lead attorney for the thousands of fishermen, Alaska Natives, property owners and others who sued the oil giant over the 11 million gallon (41.6 million litres) spill in Prince William Sound.
"We finally achieved closure at the trial court level of all aspects of this litigation," Oesting said.
The formal entry of judgment allows Exxon to appeal the trial verdict to a higher court. The company said it will enter a notice of appeal within 30 days.

"During the past two years, Exxon has raised a number of legal issues concerning the trial. Exxon's arguments on these issues have not been accepted by the Federal District Court, but we believe they establish a strong record for appeal," Exxon Chairman Lee Raymond said in a company statement.
Recent appellate and U.S. Supreme Court decisions had made Exxon optimistic about the outcome of an appeal, Raymond said.

"The puntive damages in this case are unwarranted and fail every legal or logical test of reasonableness. We believe that this judgment should be set aside or substantially reduced by the appellate court," he said.
The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals is expected to hear the case in 1997, Exxon said.
The entry of judgment also starts the accrual of interest on the $5 billion punitive award, Oesting said. The interest rate set by the court is 5.9 percent, he said.

Holland's order approved $19.5 million in compensation -- the result of the $287 million that the jury ordered in payment to approximately 10,000 commercial salmon and herring fishermen, minus credits for previous payments made by Exxon.
The order also assessed the pre-judgment interest at $37.9 million, billed to both Exxon and Hazelwood. That interest accrued on the $287 million compensatory award, Oesting said.
The totals result from a summer-long, three-phase trial conducted in Holland's court in 1994.
